newsitem.title: USA: Clinton set for re-election barring late bombshell.
newsitem.headline: Clinton set for re-election barring late bombshell.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

President Bill Clinton's performance in the final presidential debate makes it likely that barring some huge last-minute surprise event, he is headed for re-election next month, analysts said on Thursday.
"It's over unless something happens -- a real blockbuster that suddenly falls from the sky," said Daniel Hallin, communications professor at the University of California, San Diego.
Republican candidate Bob Dole boldly attacked Clinton for running an unethical administration in Wednesday's debate but the president kept smiling and refused to be drawn into a brawl.
With 19 days left until Election Day, there's little that Dole can do now except keep plugging away and hope for a miracle.

"It's hard to see how Dole will close the gap. Barring some extraordinary event, Clinton is on his way to winning the election," said John Pitney, a political scientist at Claremont McKenna College in California who once worked for the Republican Party.

National polls taken before the debate showed Clinton's lead over Dole at anything from nine to 17 percentage points. Even nine points is a substantial advantage this close the Election Day. Most striking, the Republican nominee is below 40 percent in every single national survey and has rarely approached the 40 percent mark in any poll since April.
His campaign never seemed to catch fire among an electorate which clearly feels the economy has improved in recent years and that Clinton deserves at least part of the credit.

Dole also never quite put to rest doubts about his age -- 73 -- and had to contend with voters scared by efforts of the Republican Congress in 1995 to balance the budget by cutting popular social programs.

Asked what Dole could do now, Beverly Wall, an expert on presidential debates and speeches at Trinity College in Connecticut, said: "Like a football team, you keep playing until the final second of the game even though you know you're losing. The big question is, how big will Clinton's victory be," she said.

That question becomes crucial because the focus during the final two weeks of the campaign is likely to shift to the battle for control of Congress, which the Republicans seized only two years ago but are now in danger of losing.

Most experts now give Clinton's Democrats a 50-50 chance of recapturing the House of Representatives and a somewhat lesser chance of winning back their majority in the Senate, where the party is defending a number of vulnerable seats. But much could depend on the size of Clinton's likely victory.

Reuters pollster John Zogby believes a 13 percent Clinton victory could easily translate into a Democratic victory in the House. In the Reuters daily tracking poll the president's lead Wednesday stood at 12.8 percentage points.

Arizona State University political scientist Patrick Kinney said Clinton was likely to gain around 50 percent of the popular vote and Dole could get around 40 percent, with the rest going to Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and some other minor candidates.
"The interesting question now becomes, how long are Clinton's coattails? At that kind of result, Clinton probably carries 35 states or more and the House is definitely up for grabs," he said.
Dole now faces some tough decisions. His campaign earlier this week said he intended to pour resources into a longshot effort to win California, the biggest single prize in the election.
Two recent polls put Clinton's lead in the state at 10-12 percentage points -- less than it was a few weeks ago but still formidable.

The problem with a California strategy for Dole is that TV advertising, especially in the Los Angeles area, costs more than in any other media market in the country. Money spent in California would be at the expense of other key states in the East and the Midwest, where the Republicans are defending vulnerable congressional seats.

White House political director Douglas Sosnik said Clinton had big leads in all the states where presidential elections are normally decided, including Illinois, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Iowa, Missouri and Wisconsin.

Political analyst Pitney said Dole had little to lose by putting all his chips into California. "He's better off here than in the Midwest. He's losing by a smaller margin here. But it remains the longest of long shots," he said.
